title: Array Upper Bound
statement:
Give every array a method `upperBound(target)`. It is called on an array `nums` of numbers sorted in non-decreasing order, which may hold the same value several times, and it returns the **highest index** at which `target` appears in `nums`. When `target` does not appear at all, it returns `-1`. The method belongs on `Array.prototype` so that every array has it, and it must leave the array unchanged.

Each case gives the array `nums` and the number `target`; the answer is what `nums.upperBound(target)` returns.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
Follow-up: can you do it in O(log n) time?
notes:
## Intuition

Every array inherits from `Array.prototype`, so a regular function stored there becomes a method of every array, and inside it `this` is the array it was called on. Scanning from the end and stopping at the first match (the brute force) is O(n). Because `nums` is sorted, all copies of `target` sit side by side, and the last one is just before the first element that is **greater** than `target`. Binary search finds that boundary in O(log n): the condition `this[mid] <= target` is true for a prefix of the array and false for the rest.

## Approach

1. Search the half-open range `[left, right)`, starting with `left = 0` and `right = this.length`.
2. Take the middle index `mid`. If `this[mid] <= target`, the boundary lies after `mid`, so set `left = mid + 1`; otherwise `mid` might be the boundary, so set `right = mid`.
3. When `left === right`, `left` is the first index whose value exceeds `target` (or the length).
4. `last = left - 1` is the last index whose value is at most `target`. Return it if it holds `target`, else `-1`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 4, 5]`, `target = 5`, so `left = 0`, `right = 3`.

- `mid = 1`: `4 <= 5`, so `left = 2`.
- `mid = 2`: `5 <= 5`, so `left = 3`. Now `left === right` and the loop ends.
- `last = 2` and `nums[2] = 5` equals `target`, so the answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log n): each step halves the range `[left, right)`.
- Space: O(1): a few indexes.

## Pitfalls

- Stopping at the first `mid` that equals `target` gives some copy of it, not necessarily the last one; keep moving right while values are `<= target`.
- After the loop, `left - 1` can be `-1` (every value is larger) or point at a smaller value; check that it really holds `target`.
- Despite its name, this is not C++'s `upper_bound`, which returns the first index **greater** than the target; here the answer is one before that, and only when the value matches.
- Use a regular `function`, not an arrow function, or `this` is not the array.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `this` | the sorted array `upperBound` was called on |
| `left`, `right` | the half-open range `[left, right)` still holding the boundary |
| `mid` | the middle index of that range |
| `last` | the last index whose value is at most `target` |

narration.1: Store a regular function on Array.prototype so every array gets upperBound, with this set to that array.
narration.2: The search range [left, right) starts as the whole array.
narration.3: right is one past the end, so the boundary may also be the length itself.
narration.4: Keep halving until the range shrinks to a single position.
narration.5: Look at the middle of the remaining range.
narration.6: Values up to target belong to the prefix, so the boundary is after mid.
narration.9: mid holds a larger value, so it may be the boundary; keep it in the range.
narration.12: left is now the first index with a value greater than target; the index before it is the last one at most target.
narration.13: It is the answer only if it exists and actually holds target.
narration.16: target does not appear in the array.
